title: Cast of Thousands, Serra Pelada
creator: Sebastião Salgado
body:
In 1986, Sebastião Salgado photographed workers at Serra Pelada, a gold mine in the Brazilian state of Pará. Gold discovered there in 1979 had attracted thousands of people hoping to make their fortunes. In this view, men cover the excavated ground and climb long wooden ladders, carrying the earth out in sacks.

The crowded pit had an organised division of labour. Early arrivals controlled small plots and hired others to dig, carry and wash the ore. The carriers hauled loads of roughly forty kilograms up the mine walls. Other employees counted the sacks, keeping track of work that could otherwise disappear into the crowd. Owning a plot brought the possibility of profiting from a rich find; carrying another man’s earth usually brought a wage.

Salgado’s wide view shows how much work this arrangement required. Lines of carriers extend from the bottom of the pit to its upper edges. Closer to the camera, individual men bend beneath sacks resting against their necks and shoulders. The repetition becomes easier to understand when the eye reaches one person’s load.

The photograph belongs to *Workers*, Salgado’s larger study of manual labour, published in 1993. Serra Pelada could resemble a scene from a much earlier century, but these men were producing gold for a modern market. Their labour was part of that economy, alongside the investors and buyers who did not have to climb the ladders.
meaningBrief: The mine-wide view records paid physical labour within a gold economy, not an undifferentiated crowd of independent fortune-seekers. Plot ownership, specialised jobs and the foreground carriers make the relation between opportunity, hierarchy and bodily effort understandable. The image belongs to a particular place and modern economy, not a timeless scene of suffering.

title: Children Lifting Their Empty Cups, Vienna
creator: David Seymour (Chim)
body:
Three years after the Second World War ended, schoolchildren in Vienna raise empty cups toward David Seymour’s camera. Known as Chim, the photographer made this image in 1948 for his *Children of Europe* project. Food shortages continued to shape childhood after the fighting had stopped, making a school meal part of the work of rebuilding everyday life.

In Vienna, school doctors assessed which children most needed extra food. Chim’s captions describe a programme whose limited funds covered the most underweight children and only some of the next group. UNICEF, the United Nations agency helping children, shared the cost of a daily school meal with the Austrian government. The meal was a public service supported by international aid and local resources.

Photographed from above, the children fill the frame with their faces and containers. Some look directly up; others turn aside or shade their eyes. The raised cups make the need for food immediately legible. They also bring the children into a direct exchange with the person taking their picture, rather than leaving them as distant figures in a relief report.

The project had a practical purpose: to document children’s needs and the efforts to meet them. UNESCO published *Children of Europe* in 1949. Its photographs included meals and medical care, but also games, lessons and children helping rebuild schools. Placed within that sequence, the cups belong to a larger effort to make ordinary childhood possible again.
meaningBrief: School meals show how war continued to affect children after combat ended. The visible cups connect to a documented, limited public feeding system rather than invented individual diagnoses. The institutional purpose and wider book sequence matter: food relief supports the return of education, play and everyday childhood.
